Distributions, for programmers

Discrete and continuous random variables (pmf, pdf, cdf, quantiles), the normal and the central limit theorem, the binomial and its normal approximation, the Poisson as the limit of the binomial and its overdispersion, long tails (exponential and lognormal), fitting by moments and by maximum likelihood, and how to check the fit with QQ plots and frequency tables. With scipy.stats, a from-scratch module verified against SciPy, a simulated fleet and a worked example by hand.

Summary

  • A distribution is described by its pmf (discrete) or its pdf (continuous) and, in both cases, by its cdf ; quantiles are its inverse. In SciPy: pmf/pdf, cdf, sf, ppf, isf, rvs, fit.
  • Normal : appears when adding many independent effects (CLT). With , everything reduces to : 68.3 / 95.4 / 99.7%.
  • Binomial : successes in independent trials. Mean , variance . The normal approximation fails in the tails if is small.
  • Poisson : counts of rare events in an interval; mean = variance = . If the variance exceeds the mean, there's heterogeneity: negative binomial.
  • Durations and costs usually have a long tail (lognormal; exponential for waits between Poisson events). Mean ± 2σ doesn't work there.
  • Fitting is easy; what matters is checking: QQ, observed versus expected frequencies, the var/mean index, and looking at the tails.
pmf, pdf, cdf→ normal and CLT→ binomial→ Poisson→ long tails→ fit→ check

§1 · Vocabulary

pmf, pdf, cdf and quantiles

A random variable is a number that comes out of an experiment (the fuel use of the next trip, tomorrow's alerts). If it takes separate values, it's discrete and is described by its probability mass function (pmf); if it takes values in an interval, it's continuous and is described by its density (pdf):

For a continuous variable for every , and is not a probability (it can be greater than 1): it's probability per unit, and has the inverse units of . The cdf exists for both, is non-decreasing and goes from 0 to 1; for discrete variables it jumps by . The survival function is the one used for tails, and it's best computed directly (sf) rather than as , which loses every digit when . The quantile (ppf) is the generalized inverse of ; for a discrete variable it moves in steps.

The mean and variance of a distribution are those of its values weighted by their probability (their sample versions are the ones in topic 7):

In scipy.stats each family is an object with the same methods; "freezing" it with its parameters saves repeating them. Watch out for two conventions: continuous ones use loc and scale (the normal is norm(loc=μ, scale=σ), the exponential expon(scale=1/rate), the lognormal lognorm(s, scale=e^μ)), and for discrete ones sf(k) is , so is sf(k − 1).

methodwhat it givesdiscretecontinuous
pmf(k) / pdf(x)mass or density
cdf(x)stepscontinuous
sf(x), exact in the tail
ppf(q) / isf(q)quantile of / of smallest integer with
stats(moments="mvsk")mean, variance, skewness, kurtosisclosed-form formulas
interval(c)central interval with probability (ppf((1−c)/2), ppf((1+c)/2))

basico.py · actual output

import numpy as np
from scipy import stats

consumo = stats.norm(loc=32, scale=2.5)          # L/100 km per trip: μ = 32, σ = 2.5
tarde = stats.binom(n=20, p=0.10)                # late deliveries out of 20
alertas = stats.poisson(mu=2)                    # braking alerts per truck per day

print("fuel     P(X > 37)", round(consumo.sf(37), 4), " P(30 < X < 35)", round(consumo.cdf(35) - consumo.cdf(30), 4),
      " central 95%", consumo.ppf([0.025, 0.975]).round(2))
print("late     P(X = 2)", round(tarde.pmf(2), 4), " P(X ≤ 2)", round(tarde.cdf(2), 4), " P(X ≥ 6)", round(tarde.sf(5), 4),
      " mean and variance", [float(v) for v in tarde.stats(moments="mv")])
print("alerts   P(X = 0)", round(alertas.pmf(0), 4), " P(X ≥ 7)", round(alertas.sf(6), 4),
      " 95% interval", [float(v) for v in alertas.interval(0.95)], " 99.9% quantile", float(alertas.ppf(0.999)))
print("samples", alertas.rvs(size=10, random_state=1), consumo.rvs(size=3, random_state=1).round(1))

# fuel     P(X > 37) 0.0228  P(30 < X < 35) 0.6731  central 95% [27.1 36.9]
# late     P(X = 2) 0.2852  P(X ≤ 2) 0.6769  P(X ≥ 6) 0.0113  mean and variance [2.0, 1.8]
# alerts   P(X = 0) 0.1353  P(X ≥ 7) 0.0045  95% interval [0.0, 5.0]  99.9% quantile 8.0
# samples [2 1 0 1 2 2 0 3 3 3] [36.1 30.5 30.7]

These are the numbers from the simple version: 2.3% of trips above 37 L, 67.3% between 30 and 35, 1.1% of days with 6 or more late deliveries and 0.45% of days with 7 or more alerts. The "95%" interval of the Poisson, [0, 5], actually contains 98.3% (with a discrete variable you can't cut exactly). The widget draws the pmf or pdf and the cdf of the five families in this topic.

P(X ≤ x) P(X > x) = sf(x) cdf F(x) (bottom) mean and ± one standard deviation

§2 · Normal

The bell, the z and the central limit theorem

has no closed form: it's computed with the error function (math.erf, or better erfc in the left tail) or with scipy.special.ndtr. Every normal is the standard one shifted and scaled, so a single table of is enough: , , (the 68-95-99.7 rule) and . Properties used all the time: a linear combination of independent normals is normal ( has mean and variance ), and the normal is the maximum-entropy distribution for a given mean and variance: what you assume when you only know those two numbers.

Why it shows up so often. The central limit theorem (CLT): if are independent with mean and variance ,

The second line (Berry–Esseen) says how fast it happens: the error falls like and is larger the more skewed the summands are. A trip's fuel use is the sum of many small effects (load, wind, grade, traffic): that's why it's nearly normal. Durations, which multiply, are not (§5). The z of a data point, , is the basis of the outlier rules in D4; with and estimated from the same data and heavy tails, those rules mislead (§5, §9). The multivariate normal, with its covariance matrix, is the building block of Gaussian processes and the Kalman filter.

§3 · Binomial

Successes in n trials, and when the normal approximation holds

A Bernoulli trial is 1 with probability and 0 otherwise: mean , variance . The sum of independent trials with the same is binomial. Each particular sequence with ones has probability , and there are such sequences:

Mean and variance come from adding those of the Bernoullis (the variances add because they're independent). For large , overflows: it's computed on a log scale with (math.lgamma), as in §8. Independence and a common are the assumptions that fail in practice: if a traffic jam delays several deliveries at once, delays are correlated and the real variance exceeds (overdispersion; the beta-binomial model captures it). Logistic regression is a binomial model (with per row) in which depends on the features.

Normal approximation. By the CLT, with a continuity correction: . The usual rule asks for ; with less, the binomial is skewed and the normal falls well short in the right tail:

aprox.py · actual output

import numpy as np
from scipy import stats

for n, p, k in [(20, 0.10, 6), (300, 0.10, 40), (200, 0.30, 70)]:
    mu, sd = n * p, np.sqrt(n * p * (1 - p))
    exacta = stats.binom.sf(k - 1, n, p)
    normal = stats.norm.sf((k - 0.5 - mu) / sd)               # continuity correction: P(X ≥ k) ≈ P(Y > k − 0.5)
    sin_corr = stats.norm.sf((k - mu) / sd)
    poisson = stats.poisson.sf(k - 1, mu)
    print(f"n={n:3d} p={p:.2f} P(X ≥ {k:2d})  exact {exacta:.5f}  normal+corr. {normal:.5f}  normal no corr. {sin_corr:.5f}"
          f"  Poisson {poisson:.5f}   n·p·(1−p) = {n * p * (1 - p):.1f}")

# n= 20 p=0.10 P(X ≥  6)  exact 0.01125  normal+corr. 0.00454  normal no corr. 0.00143  Poisson 0.01656   n·p·(1−p) = 1.8
# n=300 p=0.10 P(X ≥ 40)  exact 0.03780  normal+corr. 0.03375  normal no corr. 0.02715  Poisson 0.04625   n·p·(1−p) = 27.0
# n=200 p=0.30 P(X ≥ 70)  exact 0.07279  normal+corr. 0.07134  normal no corr. 0.06141  Poisson 0.11179   n·p·(1−p) = 42.0

With 20 deliveries and the normal gives 0.45% instead of 1.13%: an alarm threshold computed that way would fire 2.5 times more often than planned. With the error is already down to 2%. The Poisson with the same mean slightly overestimates the binomial's tail (its variance, , is larger than ), and is good only if is small (§4). Today there's no reason to approximate: binom.sf is exact and fast. The approximation is useful for reasoning and for quick intervals for proportions.

§4 · Poisson

Counts per interval: the limit of the binomial

Split a day into very short pieces; in each one there's an alert with probability , independently. The number of alerts is , and as the pieces become infinitely short:

Mean and variance: (the limit of and of ). The quality of the limit has a simple bound, Le Cam's inequality: the total variation distance (the largest possible difference between the probabilities they give to the same event) satisfies . It holds even if each trial has its own small , with bound : that's why the Poisson works for "many opportunities, each one rare", without knowing .

limite.py · actual output

import numpy as np
from scipy import stats

lam = 2.0; k = np.arange(0, 60)
po = stats.poisson.pmf(k, lam)
for n in (5, 10, 20, 50, 200, 1000):
    bi = stats.binom.pmf(k, n, lam / n)
    tv = 0.5 * np.abs(bi - po).sum()                 # total variation distance
    print(f"n = {n:4d}  p = {lam / n:.4f}  P(0): binomial {bi[0]:.4f}  Poisson {po[0]:.4f}   d_TV = {tv:.4f}   bound n·p² = {n * (lam / n) ** 2:.4f}")

# n =    5  p = 0.4000  P(0): binomial 0.0778  Poisson 0.1353   d_TV = 0.1249   bound n·p² = 0.8000
# n =   10  p = 0.2000  P(0): binomial 0.1074  Poisson 0.1353   d_TV = 0.0522   bound n·p² = 0.4000
# n =   20  p = 0.1000  P(0): binomial 0.1216  Poisson 0.1353   d_TV = 0.0242   bound n·p² = 0.2000

# n =  200  p = 0.0100  P(0): binomial 0.1340  Poisson 0.1353   d_TV = 0.0023   bound n·p² = 0.0200
# n = 1000  p = 0.0020  P(0): binomial 0.1351  Poisson 0.1353   d_TV = 0.0005   bound n·p² = 0.0040
Poisson(λ) Bin(n, λ/n) |difference| (bottom, ×10)

Poisson process and exponential. If events arrive at rate per hour, independently, the number in an interval of hours is , and the wait until the next one satisfies : it's exponential with mean . The sum of independent Poissons is Poisson (): the alerts of the whole fleet in a day are Poisson if each truck's are… and they share the same rate. If each driver has their own, , the count of a truck chosen at random is negative binomial:

For counts from a Poisson, approximately follows a , so the index fluctuates around 1 with standard deviation . It's the cheapest check for counts (§9). In Bayes, the Gamma is exactly the conjugate of the Poisson, and the negative binomial is its predictive distribution.

§5 · Tails

Exponential, lognormal and why mean ± 2σ fails

The third line is memorylessness, which among continuous distributions only the exponential has: having already waited 3 hours doesn't shorten what's left. It's the reference model for waits between independent events, and its standard deviation equals its mean (coefficient of variation 1). The lognormal comes from the CLT applied to a product of positive factors: tends to normal. Stop and unloading durations, repair costs and order sizes are often like this. Its skewness is : 3.7 with .

For the stops in the simple version (median 12 min, ): mean 16.5 min, standard deviation 15.6 min. A normal with that mean and standard deviation gives 14.5% negative durations and 0.27% of stops longer than 60 min, versus the real 2.2%; its 95th quantile is 42.3 min versus 44.7. The problem isn't just the tail: the normal also puts too much mass on the left. With a long tail, describe the data with the median and percentiles, or work with . There are even heavier tails, like the Pareto (power law, ), where the mean or the variance may not even exist; lognormal and power-law tails are hard to tell apart with little data (Clauset, Shalizi and Newman, 2009).

§6 · Fitting

Moments and maximum likelihood

Method of moments: set the theoretical mean (and variance) equal to the sample ones and solve. Maximum likelihood (MLE): choose the parameters that make the observed data most probable, maximizing . For these families:

familymomentsMLEnotes
normalMLE divides by ; so does norm.fit
binomial ( known)same unknown: ill-conditioned problem
Poissonsamethen compare with
exponentialsameexpon.fit(x, floc=0)
lognormal, mean and deviation (with ) of lognorm.fit(x, floc=0)

Where they coincide there's nothing to choose. For the lognormal they don't, and the difference matters: the moments depend on and , which with a long tail are dominated by a few extreme values. MLE works with logarithms, where the data is normal. Comparison over 4,000 samples of 50 stops, estimating the 95th quantile (what you promise in a service agreement):

ajuste.py · actual output

import numpy as np
from scipy import stats
from dist import ajuste_momentos, ajuste_lognormal_mv

rng = np.random.default_rng(4)
verdad = stats.lognorm(0.8, scale=12).ppf(0.95)            # true 95th quantile: 44.7 min
q95 = {"moments": [], "MLE (logs)": []}
for _ in range(4000):                                     # 4,000 samples of 50 stops
    x = rng.lognormal(np.log(12), 0.8, 50)
    for nombre, prm in [("moments", ajuste_momentos(x, "lognormal")), ("MLE (logs)", ajuste_lognormal_mv(x))]:
        q95[nombre].append(np.exp(prm["mu"] + prm["s"] * stats.norm.ppf(0.95)))
print(f"true 95th quantile: {verdad:.1f} min")
for nombre, v in q95.items():
    v = np.array(v)
    print(f"{nombre:16s} mean {v.mean():5.1f}  bias {v.mean() - verdad:+5.1f}  std. dev. {v.std():4.1f}  RMSE {np.sqrt(np.mean((v - verdad) ** 2)):4.1f}")

# true 95th quantile: 44.7 min
# moments          mean  43.4  bias  -1.4  std. dev.  8.8  RMSE  8.9
# MLE (logs)       mean  44.6  bias  -0.1  std. dev.  7.8  RMSE  7.8

MLE is almost unbiased and more precise. Even so, with 50 stops the 95th quantile has ±7.8 min of uncertainty: to promise a turnaround time it's better to give an interval (bootstrap, or the normal confidence interval of the logarithms). Two traps in scipy.stats.*.fit: without floc=0, the lognormal and the exponential also fit a shift loc, which is almost never wanted; and fit optimizes numerically, so with odd data it can return a local optimum. For discrete distributions, stats.fit(stats.nbinom, data, bounds=…). In the Bayesian view (BY) the parameters have their own distribution and MLE is the flat-prior case.

§7 · Checking

QQ plots, frequencies and goodness-of-fit tests

QQ plot. Sort the data and plot it against the theoretical quantiles of the fitted distribution. If the fit is good, the points fall on the diagonal. The shape of the deviation is diagnostic: a curve bending up at the right end is a right tail heavier than the theoretical one; a sideways "S", lighter tails (or a mix of groups); steps, rounded or discrete data. It beats the histogram because it doesn't depend on the bin width and it shows the tails, which is where the decisions are. stats.probplot does it with Filliben positions, which are nearly the same.

Frequencies. For counts, compare how often each value comes up with , grouping the tail so that each cell expects at least about 5 cases, and summarize with , with "cells − 1 − estimated parameters" degrees of freedom.

Formal tests, with care. Kolmogorov–Smirnov (kstest) measures , but its p-values assume known parameters: if they were estimated from the same data, the p comes out too large (the fix is Lilliefors, or a parametric bootstrap). With thousands of data points any test rejects deviations of no practical importance, and with few it rejects nothing: the statistic (how far off, and where) is more useful than the p-value. The widget uses the simulated data from §9.

§8 · From scratch

pmf, cdf, quantiles, sampling and fitting, verified

The essentials of each family in a few lines. Three numerical details: the normal cdf uses erfc so as not to lose digits in the left tail; the pmfs are computed in logarithms with lgamma and log1p (with , doesn't fit in a float); and the normal quantile is found by bisection, which can't diverge, plus two Newton steps. For sampling: Box–Muller (two uniforms give two normals: ), the binomial as a sum of Bernoullis, and the Poisson by sequential inversion of the cdf (cost proportional to ; NumPy uses rejection algorithms for large ).

dist.py

"""Distributions from scratch: normal, binomial, Poisson, exponential and lognormal.
pmf/pdf, cdf, quantiles, sampling and fitting by moments, with just math and numpy."""
import math
import numpy as np


# ---------- normal ----------
def norm_pdf(x, mu=0.0, sigma=1.0):
    z = (np.asarray(x, float) - mu) / sigma
    return np.exp(-0.5 * z * z) / (sigma * math.sqrt(2 * math.pi))


def norm_cdf(x, mu=0.0, sigma=1.0):
    z = (np.asarray(x, float) - mu) / (sigma * math.sqrt(2))
    return 0.5 * np.vectorize(math.erfc)(-z)                 # erfc avoids computing 1 − something in the left tail


def norm_ppf(q, mu=0.0, sigma=1.0):
    """Quantile: bisection on Φ(z) = q in [−40, 40] (60 steps) and two Newton steps to polish."""
    q = np.asarray(q, float)
    lo, hi = np.full(q.shape, -40.0), np.full(q.shape, 40.0)
    for _ in range(60):
        mid = (lo + hi) / 2
        bajo = norm_cdf(mid) < q
        lo, hi = np.where(bajo, mid, lo), np.where(bajo, hi, mid)
    z = (lo + hi) / 2
    for _ in range(2):
        z = z - (norm_cdf(z) - q) / norm_pdf(z)
    return mu + sigma * z


def norm_rvs(n, mu=0.0, sigma=1.0, rng=None):
    """Box–Muller: two uniforms give two independent normals."""
    rng = rng or np.random.default_rng()
    m = (n + 1) // 2
    u1, u2 = 1 - rng.random(m), rng.random(m)                # 1 − U ∈ (0, 1]: avoids log(0)
    r = np.sqrt(-2 * np.log(u1))
    z = np.concatenate([r * np.cos(2 * np.pi * u2), r * np.sin(2 * np.pi * u2)])[:n]
    return mu + sigma * z


# ---------- binomial ----------
def log_comb(n, k):
    return math.lgamma(n + 1) - math.lgamma(k + 1) - math.lgamma(n - k + 1)


def binom_pmf(k, n, p):
    k = np.atleast_1d(np.asarray(k))
    out = np.zeros(k.shape)
    for i, kk in enumerate(k):
        if 0 <= kk <= n:
            if p in (0.0, 1.0):
                out[i] = float(kk == (n if p == 1.0 else 0))
            else:
                out[i] = math.exp(log_comb(n, kk) + kk * math.log(p) + (n - kk) * math.log1p(-p))
    return out


def binom_cdf(k, n, p):
    return np.array([binom_pmf(np.arange(0, int(math.floor(kk)) + 1), n, p).sum() if kk >= 0 else 0.0
                     for kk in np.atleast_1d(k)])


def binom_rvs(size, n, p, rng=None):
    """Sum of n Bernoulli trials (uniform < p): direct and exact, O(n) per sample."""
    rng = rng or np.random.default_rng()
    return (rng.random((size, n)) < p).sum(axis=1)


# ---------- Poisson ----------
def pois_pmf(k, lam):
    k = np.atleast_1d(np.asarray(k, float))
    out = np.where(k >= 0, np.exp(k * math.log(lam) - lam - np.vectorize(math.lgamma)(np.maximum(k, 0) + 1)), 0.0)
    return out


def pois_cdf(k, lam):
    return np.array([pois_pmf(np.arange(0, int(math.floor(kk)) + 1), lam).sum() if kk >= 0 else 0.0
                     for kk in np.atleast_1d(k)])


def pois_rvs(size, lam, rng=None):
    """Sequential inversion: walk k = 0, 1, 2… accumulating the pmf until it passes a uniform."""
    rng = rng or np.random.default_rng()
    u = rng.random(size)
    out = np.zeros(size, int)
    p = math.exp(-lam); F = p; k = 0
    pend = np.ones(size, bool)
    while pend.any():
        hit = pend & (u <= F)
        out[hit] = k; pend &= ~hit
        k += 1; p *= lam / k; F += p
        if k > lam + 40 * math.sqrt(lam) + 40:                  # numerical safety net
            out[pend] = k; break
    return out


# ---------- exponential and lognormal ----------
def expon_cdf(x, tasa):
    return np.where(np.asarray(x) > 0, -np.expm1(-tasa * np.asarray(x, float)), 0.0)


def lognorm_pdf(x, mu, s):
    x = np.asarray(x, float)
    xs = np.where(x > 0, x, 1.0)
    return np.where(x > 0, norm_pdf(np.log(xs), mu, s) / xs, 0.0)


def lognorm_cdf(x, mu, s):
    x = np.asarray(x, float)
    return np.where(x > 0, norm_cdf(np.log(np.where(x > 0, x, 1.0)), mu, s), 0.0)


# ---------- fitting and checking ----------
def ajuste_momentos(datos, familia):
    """Parameters that make the theoretical mean (and variance) match those of the data."""
    x = np.asarray(datos, float)
    m, v = x.mean(), x.var(ddof=1)
    if familia == "normal":
        return {"mu": m, "sigma": math.sqrt(v)}
    if familia == "poisson":
        return {"lam": m}
    if familia == "binomial_p":                                # n known: data = successes out of n tries
        raise ValueError("use ajuste_binomial(datos, n)")
    if familia == "exponencial":
        return {"tasa": 1 / m}
    if familia == "lognormal":                                 # E = e^(μ+s²/2), Var = (e^(s²) − 1) E²
        s2 = math.log(1 + v / m**2)
        return {"mu": math.log(m) - s2 / 2, "s": math.sqrt(s2)}
    raise ValueError(familia)


def ajuste_binomial(datos, n):
    return {"n": n, "p": float(np.mean(datos)) / n}


def ajuste_lognormal_mv(datos):
    """Maximum likelihood: mean and deviation (with n, not n − 1) of the logarithms."""
    y = np.log(np.asarray(datos, float))
    return {"mu": y.mean(), "s": y.std()}


def qq_puntos(datos, mu=None, sigma=None):
    """Points of the normal QQ plot: theoretical quantiles at (i − 0.5)/n versus the sorted data."""
    x = np.sort(np.asarray(datos, float)); n = len(x)
    mu = x.mean() if mu is None else mu
    sigma = x.std(ddof=1) if sigma is None else sigma
    return norm_ppf((np.arange(1, n + 1) - 0.5) / n, mu, sigma), x


def tabla_frecuencias(datos, pmf, kmax):
    """Observed versus expected per value 0..kmax−1 plus a last cell "kmax or more"; χ² statistic."""
    x = np.asarray(datos); n = len(x)
    obs = np.array([np.sum(x == k) for k in range(kmax)] + [np.sum(x >= kmax)], float)
    p = np.array([pmf(k) for k in range(kmax)], float)
    esp = n * np.append(p, 1 - p.sum())
    return obs, esp, float(np.sum((obs - esp) ** 2 / esp))

The functions match SciPy to rounding level (the quantile, to even at ). The generators can't be compared number by number with NumPy's, so their moments are checked (with 200,000 samples the standard error of the mean is for the normal) along with a goodness-of-fit test: KS for the normal (here with known parameters, so it's valid) and for the Poisson. The lognormal MLE fit matches lognorm.fit(floc=0) exactly, which in that case uses the closed form; the normal fit by moments differs from norm.fit only by the factor in the standard deviation.

§9 · In the fleet

Four variables, four checks

A simulated fleet with what usually happens in real data: the fuel use of 6,000 trips from two types of truck, the alerts of 300 drivers with different rates over 60 days, 5,000 lognormal stops and 250 days of deliveries.

sim.py

"""Fleet simulator for §9: fuel use per trip, braking alerts per truck per day,
stop durations and late deliveries per day."""
import numpy as np


def flota(seed=8):
    rng = np.random.default_rng(seed)
    # fuel use (L/100 km) of 6,000 trips: 4,000 long-haul and 2,000 urban delivery
    tipo = np.r_[np.zeros(4000, int), np.ones(2000, int)]
    consumo = np.where(tipo == 0, rng.normal(32, 2.5, 6000), rng.normal(24, 2.0, 6000)).round(1)
    # harsh-braking alerts: 300 trucks × 60 days; each driver has their own rate
    tasa = rng.gamma(shape=2.0, scale=1.0, size=300)           # mean 2 alerts/day, some harsher than others
    alertas = rng.poisson(tasa[:, None], size=(300, 60))
    # duration of 5,000 stops (minutes): effects that multiply → lognormal
    paradas = rng.lognormal(np.log(12), 0.8, 5000).round(1)
    # late deliveries out of 20 per day over 250 days, p = 10%
    tarde = rng.binomial(20, 0.10, 250)
    return consumo, tipo, alertas, tasa, paradas, tarde

flota.py · actual output

import numpy as np
from scipy import stats
from sim import flota

consumo, tipo, alertas, tasa, paradas, tarde = flota()
pc = lambda v: f"{100 * v:.2f}%"

# 1. fuel use: one bell per type, two bells together
for nombre, x in [("long-haul", consumo[tipo == 0]), ("whole fleet", consumo)]:
    m, s = x.mean(), x.std(ddof=1)
    r = stats.probplot(x, dist="norm")[1][2]
    print(f"fuel {nombre:16s} mean {m:.2f}  σ {s:.2f}  within ±2σ: {pc(np.mean(abs(x - m) < 2 * s))}"
          f"  (normal: 95.45%)  QQ r {r:.4f}")
x = consumo; m, s = x.mean(), x.std(ddof=1)
print(f"  fleet: trips below 26 L/100 km  actual {pc(np.mean(x < 26))}  fitted normal {pc(stats.norm.cdf(26, m, s))}")

# 2. alerts: Poisson per truck, overdispersion across the fleet
a = alertas.ravel()
print(f"alerts: mean {a.mean():.3f}  variance {a.var(ddof=1):.3f}  var/mean index {a.var(ddof=1) / a.mean():.2f}")
idx = alertas.var(axis=1, ddof=1) / alertas.mean(axis=1)
print(f"  var/mean index of each truck (60 days): median {np.median(idx):.2f}, percentiles 5–95 {np.percentile(idx, 5):.2f}–{np.percentile(idx, 95):.2f}")
lam = a.mean()
k = a.mean() ** 2 / (a.var(ddof=1) - a.mean())               # negative binomial by moments: Var = μ + μ²/k
nb = stats.nbinom(k, k / (k + lam))
for umbral in (7, 10):
    print(f"  days with ≥ {umbral:2d} alerts  actual {pc(np.mean(a >= umbral))}  Poisson({lam:.2f}) {pc(stats.poisson.sf(umbral - 1, lam))}"
          f"  negative binomial (k = {k:.2f}) {pc(nb.sf(umbral - 1))}")
tot = alertas.sum(axis=1)
p_cam = stats.poisson.sf(tot - 1, 60 * lam)                  # P(≥ the truck's total) if all had the mean rate
print(f"  trucks with P(≥ their total | mean rate) < 0.001: {np.sum(p_cam < 0.001)} of 300; their actual mean rate {tasa[p_cam < 0.001].mean():.2f}")

# 3. stops: normal versus lognormal
m, s = paradas.mean(), paradas.std(ddof=1)
sl, _, esc = stats.lognorm.fit(paradas, floc=0)
print(f"stops: mean {m:.1f} min  median {np.median(paradas):.1f}  σ {s:.1f}  skewness {stats.skew(paradas):.2f}")
print(f"  lognormal MLE: median e^μ = {esc:.2f} min, s = {sl:.3f}")
for nombre, F in [("normal (moments)", stats.norm(m, s)), ("lognormal (MLE)", stats.lognorm(sl, scale=esc))]:
    print(f"  {nombre:18s} P(< 0) {pc(F.cdf(0)):>8s}  P(> 60 min) {pc(F.sf(60)):>7s}  95th quantile {F.ppf(0.95):5.1f}  KS {stats.kstest(paradas, F.cdf).statistic:.3f}")
print(f"  data               P(< 0) {pc(0.0):>8s}  P(> 60 min) {pc(np.mean(paradas > 60)):>7s}  95th quantile {np.percentile(paradas, 95):5.1f}")

# 4. late deliveries: observed frequencies versus binomial(20, p̂)
p_hat = tarde.mean() / 20
obs = np.append(np.bincount(tarde, minlength=6)[:6], np.sum(tarde >= 6))
esp = 250 * np.append(stats.binom.pmf(np.arange(6), 20, p_hat), stats.binom.sf(5, 20, p_hat))
chi = stats.chisquare(obs, esp, ddof=1)
print(f"late deliveries: p̂ = {p_hat:.4f}   observed {obs.tolist()}   expected {esp.round(1).tolist()}")
print(f"  χ² = {chi.statistic:.2f}, p = {chi.pvalue:.2f} (5 degrees of freedom: 7 cells − 1 − estimated p)")

# fuel long-haul        mean 32.00  σ 2.55  within ±2σ: 95.35%  (normal: 95.45%)  QQ r 0.9998
# fuel whole fleet      mean 29.33  σ 4.48  within ±2σ: 98.08%  (normal: 95.45%)  QQ r 0.9831
#   fleet: trips below 26 L/100 km  actual 28.27%  fitted normal 22.88%
# alerts: mean 2.184  variance 4.628  var/mean index 2.12
#   var/mean index of each truck (60 days): median 0.98, percentiles 5–95 0.73–1.34
#   days with ≥  7 alerts  actual 4.42%  Poisson(2.18) 0.72%  negative binomial (k = 1.95) 4.67%
#   days with ≥ 10 alerts  actual 1.05%  Poisson(2.18) 0.01%  negative binomial (k = 1.95) 0.90%
#   trucks with P(≥ their total | mean rate) < 0.001: 78 of 300; their actual mean rate 4.16
# stops: mean 16.8 min  median 11.9  σ 16.3  skewness 3.18
#   lognormal MLE: median e^μ = 12.05 min, s = 0.812
#   normal (moments)   P(< 0)   15.11%  P(> 60 min)   0.40%  95th quantile  43.6  KS 0.171
#   lognormal (MLE)    P(< 0)    0.00%  P(> 60 min)   2.40%  95th quantile  45.8  KS 0.012
#   data               P(< 0)    0.00%  P(> 60 min)   2.72%  95th quantile  48.0
# late deliveries: p̂ = 0.1048   observed [29, 65, 66, 55, 17, 15, 3]   expected [27.3, 63.9, 71.1, 50.0, 24.9, 9.3, 3.5]
#   χ² = 7.03, p = 0.22 (5 degrees of freedom: 7 cells − 1 − estimated p)

Fuel use: one bell per group. Long-haul trips are normal (95.35% within ±2σ, QQ coefficient 0.9998). Mixed with the delivery trips, the "fleet σ" (4.48) describes no one: there are two bells, ±2σ contains 98%, and the fitted normal gets the concrete questions wrong (22.9% of trips below 26 L versus the real 28.3%). Before fitting a shape, separate the groups you know are different.

Alerts: Poisson per driver, negative binomial across the fleet. The var/mean index of each truck is around 1 (median 0.98; with 60 days you expect ), but the fleet's is 2.12. A Poisson with the fleet mean predicts 0.72% of days with 7 or more alerts; there are 4.42%. The negative binomial fitted by moments (, very close to the 2 in the simulation) gets it right. The practical takeaway: the "unusual day" threshold has to be computed per driver, with their own ; with the fleet's, 78 of the 300 drivers come out "anomalous" with , and they aren't trucks with unusual days but drivers with a higher rate (4.2 on average).

Stops: long tail. Skewness 3.2, mean 16.8 versus median 11.9. The normal gives 15% negative durations and 0.4% of stops longer than an hour (there are 2.7%); its KS is 0.171. The lognormal by MLE: 2.4% and KS 0.012.

Late deliveries: binomial is right. With , observed and expected agree reasonably well ( with 5 degrees of freedom, ): there's no reason to reject the binomial, which is all that test says.

§10 · Checklist

Before you trust a distribution

  • Choose the family from how the data is generated (counted or measured? is there a fixed ? sum or product? a lower bound?) and then check it against the data, not the other way around.
  • Separate known groups (truck type, route, driver) before fitting: a mixture is none of the families.
  • For counts, compare variance and mean. An index clearly above 1: negative binomial, or model each unit's rate.
  • Compute tails with sf/isf and remember that for discrete distributions sf(k) is .
  • With a long tail, describe with the median and percentiles, fit in logarithms and don't use mean ± 2σ as a threshold.
  • Set floc=0 when fitting a lognormal or exponential with fit, unless the shift has a physical meaning.
  • Look at the QQ plot (or the frequencies) in the tails; don't decide on the KS p-value alone, least of all with estimated parameters.
  • If a threshold is based on the distribution, measure afterwards how often it actually fires and compare with what was expected.

§11 · Worked example

Fuel use, late deliveries and alerts, by hand

The numbers from the simple version, computed without a computer: two questions about the normal for fuel use, the binomial for late deliveries with its cost in dollars, the Poisson for alerts and its relation to the binomial, and the estimate of from ten days of data.

The setup. The operations manager wants three things: to know whether a 37 L/100 km trip calls for an inspection, to budget late-delivery penalties, and to set a braking-alert threshold that doesn't fire by pure chance.

Example map

Three fleet variables with their distributions: the fuel used on each trip, normal with and L/100 km; the late deliveries in a day, binomial with and ; and a truck's braking alerts, Poisson with . At the end, how to estimate from ten days of data.

  1. Normal: the z of a 37 L trip and its probability.
  2. Normal: a range, between 30 and 35 L.
  3. Binomial: counting the ways k can arrive late.
  4. Binomial: mean, variance and cost in dollars.
  5. Binomial: is a day with 6 late rare?
  6. Poisson: the probability of each number of alerts.
  7. Poisson and binomial: the same mean, almost the same shape.
  8. Estimating λ from ten days and checking the variance.

  1. Normal: the z of a 37 L trip

    In words

    To know whether a trip that uses 37 L/100 km is rare, you measure how many standard deviations it is from the average fuel use (that's ) and look up in the standard normal table what share of trips lies above it.

    The math

    Where does each number come from?

    is the average fuel use of long-haul trips and its standard deviation (topic 7), in L/100 km; has no units. is the probability that a standard normal falls below 2: it comes from a table or from norm.cdf(2). The 68-95-99.7 rule gives it almost without a table: 95.4% lies within ±2σ, 4.6% outside, and half of that above, 2.3%.

    What it means: 1 in 44 trips uses this much or more by chance. Those 5 extra liters per 100 km, on a 600 km trip, are 30 L; at $1.65/L, $49.50. One trip like this is no alarm; several in a row from the same truck are.

  2. Normal: a range, between 30 and 35 L

    The math

    Why a subtraction?

    is the area to the left of 35 L and the area to the left of 30 L; what's left between them is the difference. Tables usually list only : by symmetry, , which is .

    What it means: two trips out of three use between 30 and 35 L: it's the 67.3% orange area from idea 1 of the simple version. An exact value, such as 32.000 L, has probability 0: only ranges have area.

  3. Binomial: counting the ways k can arrive late

    In words

    Each of the 20 deliveries arrives late with probability 0.1, without affecting the others. One particular list with delays has probability , and there are different lists with delays.

    The math

    Where does the 190 come from?

    : there are 20 ways to choose the first delivery that's late and 19 for the second, and you divide by 2 because the order doesn't matter (number 3 and number 7 is the same as 7 and 3). is "all 20 on time": 0.9 multiplied 20 times.

    What it means: two days out of three have at most 2 late deliveries. These are the three orange bars from idea 1 of the simple version: 12.2 + 27.0 + 28.5 = 67.7%.

  4. Binomial: mean, variance and cost in dollars

    The math

    Where does each factor come from?

    Each delivery contributes, on average, 0.1 delays (it's 1 with probability 0.1 and 0 with 0.9), and the mean of a sum is the sum of the means: . The variance of a single delivery is ; since they're independent, the variances add up too: . The $15 is the contract's penalty per late delivery, and 250 is the number of workdays in the year.

    What it means: the annual penalty budget is $7,500. The standard deviation of 1.34 delays per day says how much each day wobbles around those 2.

  5. Binomial: is a day with 6 late rare?

    The math

    Why through the complement?

    "6 or more" is 15 cases (6, 7, …, 20) with tiny probabilities; "5 or fewer" is 6 cases, and four were already computed. The coefficients are , and . In SciPy, binom.sf(5, 20, 0.1): careful, sf(5) is .

    What it means: a day with 6 or more delays happens 1.13% of the time: in 250 days, about days a year by pure chance. If it happens every week, the model "each delivery goes its own way with p = 0.1" no longer holds: something has changed.

  6. Poisson: the probability of each number of alerts

    In words

    A truck gives on average harsh-braking alerts a day. With the Poisson formula, each probability comes from the previous one by multiplying by .

    The math

    Where does each constant come from?

    is the base of natural logarithms: is the probability of a day with no alerts at all, the limit of when you split the day into tiny pieces (§4). counts the possible orders of the alerts. The sum from to is 0.9955.

    What it means: with 7 or more alerts as the threshold, the alert fires by chance on 0.45% of days, 1 in 221: with 300 trucks, a little more than 1 alert a day across the whole fleet. With a threshold of 5 it would fire on 5.3% of days: 16 alerts a day, most of them false alarms.

  7. Poisson and binomial: the same mean, almost the same shape

    Comparison, k = 0 to 4

    kBin(20, 0.1)Pois(2)
    00.1220.135
    10.2700.271
    20.2850.271
    30.1900.180
    40.0900.090

    Why are they alike?

    Both have mean 2. The binomial is a Poisson with "only" 20 opportunities: it has a bit less variance (1.8 versus 2) and therefore fewer days at the extremes (0.122 versus 0.135 at 0). With 200 opportunities of the difference almost disappears: 0.134 versus 0.135. Le Cam's bound, , is 0.2 with and 0.02 with .

    What it means: for alerts you don't need to know how many times a truck brakes or the probability of each one: the mean is enough. That's why the Poisson is the default model for counts of rare events.

  8. Estimating λ from ten days and checking the variance

    In words

    A new truck has given these alerts in its first ten days: 2, 1, 0, 1, 2, 2, 0, 3, 3, 3 (they are the ten samples from basico.py). The best value of , by moments and by maximum likelihood, is the mean. If it really is Poisson, the variance should be close to the mean.

    The math

    Where does each number come from?

    17 is the sum of the ten figures. Each term of the sum is : for example, and . You divide by (topic 7). With ten data points, the index of a Poisson fluctuates around 1 with standard deviation , so 0.79 is perfectly compatible.

    What it means: there's no reason to doubt the Poisson, and this driver is somewhat below the fleet average (1.7 versus 2). With , the 7-alert threshold would fire on 0.19% of days. But ten days isn't much: that λ can still move quite a bit, and it's worth reviewing after a month.

ejemplo.py · reproduces the numbers above

import math
import numpy as np
from scipy import stats

# 1–2. normal: fuel use μ = 32, σ = 2.5 L/100 km
z = (37 - 32) / 2.5; print("z =", z, " P(X > 37) =", round(stats.norm.sf(z), 4), " 30 L × $1.65 =", 30 * 1.65)
za, zb = (30 - 32) / 2.5, (35 - 32) / 2.5
print("z:", za, zb, " Φ:", round(stats.norm.cdf(zb), 4), round(stats.norm.cdf(za), 4), " P(30 < X < 35) =", round(stats.norm.cdf(zb) - stats.norm.cdf(za), 4))
# 3–5. binomial: 20 deliveries, p = 0.1
p = [math.comb(20, k) * 0.1**k * 0.9**(20 - k) for k in range(8)]
print("C(20,k):", [math.comb(20, k) for k in range(6)], " 0.9^20, 0.9^19, 0.9^18:", round(0.9**20, 4), round(0.9**19, 4), round(0.9**18, 4))
print("P(k), k = 0..5:", [round(v, 4) for v in p[:6]], " P(≤ 2) =", round(sum(p[:3]), 4), " P(≤ 5) =", round(sum(p[:6]), 4), " P(≥ 6) =", round(1 - sum(p[:6]), 4))
print("mean", 20 * 0.1, " variance", round(20 * 0.1 * 0.9, 2), " σ", round(math.sqrt(1.8), 3), " cost/day", 2 * 15, " 250 days", 250 * 2 * 15, " days with ≥ 6:", round(250 * (1 - sum(p[:6])), 1))
# 6–7. Poisson λ = 2 and the binomial that resembles it
q = [math.exp(-2) * 2**k / math.factorial(k) for k in range(8)]
print("Poisson P(k), k = 0..6:", [round(v, 4) for v in q[:7]], " P(≥ 7) =", round(1 - sum(q[:7]), 4), " e^-2 =", round(math.exp(-2), 4))
print("binomial(20, 0.1) versus Poisson(2), k = 0..4:", [(round(a, 3), round(b, 3)) for a, b in zip(p[:5], q[:5])])
print("binomial(200, 0.01): P(0) =", round(0.99**200, 4))
# 8. estimate λ from 10 days of one truck
x = np.array([2, 1, 0, 1, 2, 2, 0, 3, 3, 3])
print("sum", x.sum(), " λ̂ =", x.mean(), " squared deviations", ((x - x.mean())**2).round(2).tolist(), " sum", round(((x - x.mean())**2).sum(), 2),
      " s² =", round(x.var(ddof=1), 3), " s²/λ̂ =", round(x.var(ddof=1) / x.mean(), 2), " ±", round(math.sqrt(2 / 9), 2))
print("P(≥ 7 | λ̂ = 1.7) =", round(stats.poisson.sf(6, 1.7), 4))

What would change in a real system

  • Estimated parameters, not known ones: μ, σ, p and λ come from data and carry uncertainty; with few days, a "0.45%" threshold may really be 0.2% or 1%.
  • One bell per group: the reference fuel use depends on truck model, route and load (§9).
  • Independence: delays and alerts cluster (a traffic jam, roadworks). Look at the var/mean index before trusting the binomial or the Poisson.
  • Review the thresholds: count how often they actually fire and compare with what was expected.
